opus-5.5.text:
Well, mostly on our own experiments. My group has been working on planning and reasoning with these models for a few years now, and we built PlanBench precisely so that we wouldn't have to rely on anecdotes or on whatever the companies chose to put in their blog posts. When o1-preview came out, we ran it on the same benchmark we had used for GPT-4, Claude, and the rest.

And to be fair, it's a real improvement. On the standard Blocksworld problems, where the autoregressive models had plateaued, o1 does dramatically better, close to saturating it. On Mystery Blocksworld, where we obfuscate the domain names so you can't just retrieve what you've seen on the web, the earlier models were in the low single digits, essentially nothing. o1 gets a meaningful fraction right, something like half. So I'm not one of those people who'll say nothing has changed. Something has.

But then you look more carefully. Performance degrades quickly as problems get longer. When we give it unsolvable problems, it often confidently produces a "plan" anyway, or gives a wrong rationale for why it can't be solved. And it costs a lot. You pay for all those reasoning tokens you can't even see, and the latency is significant. When you compare that to a classical planner like Fast Downward, which solves these instances correctly, with guarantees, in a fraction of a second at essentially zero cost, you have to ask what you're actually buying.

So my judgments rest on three things: systematic evaluation on problems where we control the distribution, especially ones designed to defeat retrieval; looking at failure modes, not just accuracy numbers; and accounting for cost and guarantees, not just the headline score. I call these large reasoning models rather than LLMs because they're clearly doing something beyond pure autoregressive generation, probably some kind of RL-trained search over generated reasoning traces. But as for whether they "reason" in the sense we'd want for deploying them where correctness matters, the evidence says not yet. That's why I keep arguing for LLM-modulo setups, where these models generate candidates and sound external verifiers check them.

r001.rationale: He says his judgments are based mostly on his group’s experiments, including running o1-preview on PlanBench across planning problems, and explicitly contrasts systematic evaluation with relying on anecdotes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I base them on what we can actually test, because that's really all any of us have to go on. OpenAI has been quite opaque about what O1 is doing under the hood. They talk about "reasoning tokens" and reinforcement learning on chains of thought, but they don't show you the chains, and they don't tell you how the training was done. So you have to treat it as a black box and poke at it from the outside.

My group has been doing this for a while now with planning benchmarks, in particular Blocks World and the obfuscated version, which we call Mystery Blocks World. These are problems where we have a verifier. We know whether a plan is correct, so there's no hand-waving about whether the answer "sounds reasonable." When we ran O1 on these, we saw a genuine jump compared to the earlier LLMs. On Blocks World it went from something like the low thirties to the high nineties on the standard instances. That's real, and I said so publicly. I'm not in the business of denying improvement when it's there.

But then you look at the details. On the obfuscated version, where the predicate names are scrambled so you can't lean on surface patterns, the performance drops substantially. And when you increase the plan length, it falls off a cliff again, just at a later point than GPT-4 did. So what you're seeing is something that looks a lot like approximate retrieval combined with some amount of learned search heuristics, rather than a system that actually does sound reasoning in the sense that a planner does. It's an "LRM," a large reasoning model, if you like, and I think that's a fair label, but you should understand what it is and isn't.

The other thing is cost. O1 was spending a huge amount of compute on these problems, and when we compared it to a classical planner like Fast Downward, the planner solves all of them in milliseconds and gets them all right. So whenever someone tells me O1 is "reasoning," my question is always: measured how, on what distribution, and against what baseline? If the answer is "it did well on a benchmark that was probably in the training data," I'm not that impressed. If it's "it does well on instances with guarantees, out of distribution, at scale," then we should talk. We're just not there yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Kambhampati bases his judgments on external testing and describes his group evaluating O1 on planning benchmarks with verified instances, rather than relying on everyday-use anecdotes.

astra-6.text:
I base them on what the system can actually do on problems where we can check the answer, particularly planning problems. Does it produce a valid plan? Does that performance hold up when you change the problem, rather than just change the wording of the prompt?

I would separate that from how convincing its explanation sounds. A system can give you a very plausible account of its reasoning and still produce an incorrect answer. So the important evidence is independent verification of the result, across a range of problems—not the system’s own description of how it got there.

And there are two different questions: has O1 improved performance, and what does that improvement establish about its reasoning capabilities? You can acknowledge the first without assuming you’ve settled the second.

r001.rationale: The response bases its judgments on independently checked performance across a range of planning problems, including whether valid plans generalize to changed problems. That communicates evaluation across multiple instances rather than reliance on everyday anecdotes.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the key question is whether it can reliably solve problems where we can independently check the answer. If we’re talking about planning, for example, does the proposed plan actually achieve the goal while respecting the constraints? A convincing explanation is not enough. I would want to see systematic evaluations, comparisons with other models, and tests of how performance changes as the problems become harder. And I would distinguish the capability of the model itself from the capability of a system that gives it tools, feedback, and multiple attempts.

r001.rationale: The response bases judgments on systematic evaluations of planning problems, including tests across increasing difficulty. That communicates evaluation across multiple instances rather than relying on everyday anecdotes.
